procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court initiated Suo Moto Contempt Petition (Criminal) No.5 of 2017 against an Advocate-on-Record (the contemnor) based on a letter/grievance submitted to the Chief Justice of India. The court issued a summons to the Advocate-on-Record to show cause against the allegations made in the summons. The allegations suggest the Advocate-on-Record engaged in 'bench hunting' by making unreasonable mentioning of the matter before the court under the guise of representing the client's interest.

issue.issue_text: Whether a matter could be put on the board without notice to other parties after its deletion from the list.

facts: On March 31, 2017, the Court issued a specific judicial direction for the matter to be listed for a final hearing on April 7, 2017.
The matter was inadvertently deleted from the advance cause list but was subsequently re-listed for April 7, 2017, in accordance with the prior judicial order.
An advocate alleged that this re-listing was unnatural, hasty, without sufficient notice, and constituted an act of "bench hunting" by the Registry.
application: The Court found the advocate's allegations to be "palpably false."
The Court reasoned that because of the specific judicial order from March 31st, no party could have been taken by surprise by the listing on April 7th. This prior order served as sufficient notice.
The deletion from the advance list was deemed an inadvertent error, and its correction by re-listing the matter was simply the implementation of the Court's own directive.
The Court also clarified that the case was listed before the regular bench that had passed the prior order, not a "special bench" as was falsely alleged.

The Court concluded that the advocate's complaint was not a genuine issue of being unaware of the listing but was, in fact, an endeavor at "bench hunting" to prevent the case from being heard by that specific bench.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the matter was improperly put on the board. It held that the listing was based on a prior judicial direction which provided sufficient notice to the parties, and the re-listing after an inadvertent deletion was therefore not surprising or improper.

issue.issue_text: Whether the matter was listed in unnatural haste, without sufficient notice, and before a special bench deviating from the regular bench, in violation of judicial propriety.

facts: On March 31, 2017, a specific court order was issued directing the matter to be listed for a final hearing on April 7, 2017.
The matter was listed on April 7, 2017, before the very same bench that had passed the March 31 order.
The bench in question was the regular bench, not a specially constituted one.
The lawyer making the allegations (the contemnor) had re-entered the case after a previous Advocate-on-Record had seemingly refused to make such unreasonable requests to the court.
application: The Supreme Court found the allegations that the matter was listed in haste and before a special bench to be "palpably false."

The Court reasoned that because of the prior order on March 31, which scheduled the April 7 hearing, no party could genuinely claim to be surprised or to have had insufficient notice, even if the case was inadvertently deleted from and then re-added to the list.
The Court directly refuted the claim of a "special bench," stating that there was no change in the bench and it was the regular bench assigned to the matter.

The Court concluded that the allegations were not a legitimate grievance but were, in fact, an improper attempt by the litigant and their lawyer to engage in "bench hunting"—the practice of trying to get a case moved away from a particular judge or bench.

The Court described the lawyer's actions as a "conscious decision to be a pawn in the hands of the litigant, to scandalize the Court and the Registry... with the sole objective of achieving a bench shifting."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the issue, determining that the claims were factually incorrect. The Court found that the matter was properly listed before the regular bench with sufficient notice based on a prior order, and that the allegations were a bad-faith attempt at "bench hunting" by the lawyer and their client.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a matter could be put on the board without notice to other parties after its deletion from the list.
appellant_arguments: The advocate (contemnor) argued that making a special mention before the court was the 'only course available' to him, implying that the re-listing of the case after its deletion from the advance list was improper and done without adequate notice.
respondent_arguments: The court found that the advocate's averments were 'palpably false'. It reasoned that even if the matter was inadvertently deleted from the advance list, its reappearance was 'not surprising' given the last court order. It was not a genuine case of an advocate being unaware of the listing and unable to represent his client.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the matter was listed in unnatural haste, without sufficient notice, and before a special bench deviating from the regular bench, in violation of judicial propriety.
appellant_arguments: The advocate (contemnor) made 'insinuations and allegations' that the case was improperly placed before a 'Special Bench' and that there was a 'change in the Bench', suggesting a violation of judicial propriety.
respondent_arguments: The court found these allegations to be 'palpably false'. It clarified that 'There was no change in the Bench nor case had been placed before the Special Bench, as alleged'. The court concluded that the contemnor was brought in by the petitioner to engage in 'bench hunting, under the garb of allegations and insinuations' after the previous advocate refused to make such unreasonable requests.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The advocate's actions were not an innocent endeavor but a calculated, well-thought-out decision to make false allegations against the Registry and cast innuendoes against the Court. The objective was to assist the client by improperly seeking a shift of the Bench, a path the previous advocate was unwilling to take. This conduct was an abuse of the privilege of being an Advocate-on-Record and was unbecoming of an advocate.
legal_tests_applied: An advocate's duty as an officer of the Court is to aid and assist in the administration of justice, which is distinct from the duty to the client to legitimately present their side of the case.
The fundamentals of the profession require an advocate not to be immersed in a blind quest of relief for his client, as the dignity of the institution cannot be violated in this quest.

A lawyer must not render any service or advice involving disloyalty to the law, disrespect of the judicial office, or deception, and will find his highest honor in a deserved reputation for fidelity to private trust and to public duty.
why_appellant_lost: The court found that the advocate's allegations against the Registry were false and that there were innuendoes against the Court.

The court determined that the advocate's actions were not an 'innocent act' or an 'innocuous endeavor' but a 'well thought out decision to tread an unfortunate path which the existing Advocate-on-Record was unwilling to do.'
The court concluded that the advocate's true objective was 'only to assist the client by somehow seeking shifting of the Bench.'
The advocate's conduct was found to be an abuse of the 'privilege of being an Advocate-on-Record' and was 'not becoming of an advocate much less an advocate-on-record in the Supreme Court.'
why_respondent_won: The court established that the advocate's allegations were false and made with the oblique motive of 'bench hunting.'
The court reasoned that the contempt jurisdiction extends to protecting the Registry from false and unfair allegations that seek to impede the administration of justice.
The court's position was reinforced by the principle that an advocate's duty to uphold the dignity of the institution and the administration of justice is paramount, even over the client's interests.
policy_considerations: The contempt jurisdiction is not only to protect the reputation of the concerned Judge so that he can administer Justice fearlessly and fairly, but also to protect 'the fair name of the judiciary'. The protection... extends even to the Registry in the performance of its task and false and unfair allegations which seek to impede the working of the Registry and thus the administration of Justice, made with oblique motives cannot be tolerated.

The fundamentals of the profession require an advocate not to be immersed in a blind quest of relief for his client. The dignity of the institution cannot be violated in this quest as 'law is no trade, briefs no merchandise'.

No client, corporate or individual, however powerful, nor any cause civil or political, however important, is entitled to receive, nor should any lawyer render, any service or advice involving disloyalty to the law whose ministers we are, or disrespect of the judicial office, which we are bound to uphold.
